newsitem.title: USA: Con Edison settlement faces court test.
newsitem.headline: Con Edison settlement faces court test.

text.p: The settlement Consolidated Edison Co of New York Inc reached after negotiations on its competitive opportunities filing faces a court challenge if approved by the state Public Service Commission, a New York Assembly hearing was told Friday.

"The agreement lays the foundation for the most significant change in the way electric service is provided in the metropolitan area in the last half century," Con Edison told the hearing called by the Assembly committees on Energy, Corporations and Consumer Afairs.
Those opposed to the settlement told the hearing the agreement fails to meet its stated objective of providing "meaningful rate reduction."
They said it also fails to establish a level playing field for competition and "ignores the reality that retail access is technically feasible for all customers."

As a result "the settlement offers no hope of cost reductions or service enhancements through competition," Aaron Breidenbauch, the Independent Power Producers of New York's deputy director and director of regulatory affairs, said.

Others questioned on why the settlement discriminates between customers classes, giving the largest -- 25 percent -- cuts to an estimated 20 industrial customers in an area that no longer depends on industrial activity for economic growth.
Several joined Energy Committee chairman Paul D. Tonko in questioning the process by which the agreement was reached.

It appears to have been "negotiated directly by senior Department of Public Service staff and senior Con Ed officials," Breidenbaugh said, asserting the utility "struck a bargain (to make) token rate reductions in return for withdrawal" from suit challenging the restructuring process.

Later, he told Reuters all three utilities reaching a restructuring settlement -- Central Hudson Gas & Electric Corp, Orange & Rockland Utilities Inc and Con Edison -- agreed to withdraw from the New York Energy Association's lawsuit challenging the Public Service Commission's May 1996 Competitive Opportunities order.
That order now "appears to be nothing more than a dim memory," Tonko said.
New York Public Interest Research Group's senior attorney, Larry Shapiro, said he believes "deals were made."
It "appears this plan will allow Con Ed to do less than other companies" who have settled with the commission, American Association of Retired Persons legislative representative Travis Plunkett said.
Assemblyman Richard L. Brodsky, chairman of the Assembly Environmental Committee, said "this is corporate welfare."

"It's my belief a deal was cut by (Commission Chairman John) O'Mara and (Con Edison chief executive Eugene) McGrath in a room," he said. Con Edison corporate planning vice president Kevin "Burke did not answer the questions (about the talks that led to the pact) to my satisfaction," Brodksy said.
"Nor to ours," Tonko said. During Burke's testimony he requested the utility official to provide information in writing about participants in the negotiations.
Brodsky, who represents part of Con Edison's service territory north of New York City, suggested that the information be supoenaed.

But Shapiro, like Burke a participant in the negotiations, suggested the Con Edison official "went over the line" on the confidentiality agreement covering the talks. Shapiro declined to discuss the talks because of that agreement.
If the settlement "plays out solely before the PSC, it will be litigated," he said.
"There will more than likely be low suits by concerned parties," Tonko agreed, citing the unequal treatment of various groups by the settlement.
It will go to court after the commission rules in June, the Assemblyman said, explaining he does not see the commission making the needed adjustments in Con Edison's revenue flow.
It appears the settlement "will be approved as written" by the commission, Breidenbaugh said.
"If so, it will be challenged in court," he said, adding the commission "will get a stay and (the Con Edison settlement) will go into effect.

"Our hope is the commission will see the light" and make the changes to bring Con Edison's restructuring back into line with the proposals the regulators laid down in May 1996, Breidenbaugh said. ((-- New York Newsdesk 212-859-1610))
